about: Built-in positions library for Chess Views. Each entry has a fen (six fields) or a pgn with a ply, a name, a short note for the kid and the parent, tags, and the view it is best seen in.

positions.name: Start position
positions.note: Where every game begins. Try each view on it: who controls the centre before anyone has moved?

positions.name: Italian Game
positions.note: Both bishops aim at the weakest squares on the board, f7 and f2, which only the kings defend. Roads shows the two diagonals.

positions.name: London System
positions.pgn: 1. d4 d5 2. Bf4 Nf6 3. e3 e6 4. Nf3 c5 5. c3 Nc6 6. Nbd2 Bd6 7. Bg3 O-O 8. Bd3
positions.note: The bishop comes out to f4 before e3 shuts it in; then c3 and e3 make a pawn pyramid around d4. White plays this against almost anything. Step back through the moves: the bishop keeps its diagonal the whole way.

positions.name: Scholar's mate threat
positions.note: White threatens Qxf7 mate. Territory shows f7 attacked twice with only the king to guard it. Black to move: how do you stop it?

positions.name: Alapin structure
positions.note: From the blog post 'How Masters See the Board': a d4-e5 pawn chain against a fianchetto. Shapes turns it into the chunking exercise.

positions.name: Isolated queen's pawn
positions.note: White's d-pawn has no pawn neighbours. It gives space and open roads now, and becomes a weakness in the endgame. Black to move.

positions.name: French pawn chains
positions.note: Advance French. The chains d4-e5 and d5-e6 lock the centre. Black attacks the base with ...c5, and Black's light bishop is shut in.

positions.name: Carlsbad structure
positions.note: White's plan is the minority attack: b4 and b5 to make c6 weak. Black plays for ...Ne4 and a push on the kingside.

positions.name: Two fianchetto houses
positions.note: Both kings live behind a fianchetto. King houses shows how the g-bishop holds the house together, and what is missing if it gets traded.

positions.name: King trap study
positions.note: White to move. Black's king is boxed in by its own pieces, but careless White moves are stalemate. Which moves keep the win?

positions.name: Back-rank mate
positions.note: Mate in one. The pawns that shield the king also lock it in, and the back rank is open. Look in King houses, then find it in Reach.

positions.name: Queen mate
positions.note: King and queen against king. Shrink the box with the queen, walk your king up, and never take the last square away: that is stalemate.

positions.name: Rook mate
positions.note: King and rook against king. Cut the king off with the rook, then push it to the edge with your own king.

positions.name: King in front of its pawn
positions.note: The white king stands two squares ahead of its pawn, so White wins whoever is to move. Reach shows how few squares the black king has.

positions.name: Stalemate, no move left
positions.note: White to move, not in check, and no legal move: stalemate, a draw. Black was a pawn from winning. Reach paints the stuck king grey.

positions.name: Mate or stalemate?
positions.note: White to move. Some queen moves are mate, one of them (Qf7) is stalemate. Reach marks the ½ squares: find them before you move.

positions.name: Lucena bridge
positions.note: Rook endgame. Rd1+ pushes the black king away, then Rd4 builds the bridge so your rook can block the checks on the 4th rank.

positions.name: Knight fork
positions.note: Find the knight move that gives check and attacks the rook at the same time. Click the knight to see its tracks.

positions.name: Bishop pins the knight
positions.note: Black's bishop on g4 pins the knight to the queen. Reach shows the open padlock: the knight may move, but it would cost the queen.

positions.name: Knight in the corner
positions.note: Turn on hop counts. How many hops from the corner to the other corner? Which squares are farthest from the knight?

positions.name: Mate in three (a real problem)
positions.pgn:
[Event "White to play and mate in three"]
[FEN "8/1n4K1/qpB4p/3R3P/4kp1N/2p4P/2P1pP2/6R1 w - - 0 1"]
[SetUp "1"]

1. Rf1 b5 2. f3+ Ke3 3. Rd3#
positions.note: From NM ZugAddict's blog: solve a real composed problem, not a tactics-trainer one. Set it up on a real board. The moves are hidden; find White's first move, then press ▶ to check. Hint: it is a quiet move.

positions.name: Morphy's Opera game
positions.pgn:
[White "Morphy"]
[Black "Duke of Brunswick and Count Isouard"]

1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 Bg4 4. dxe5 Bxf3 5. Qxf3 dxe5 6. Bc4 Nf6 7. Qb3 Qe7 8. Nc3 c6 9. Bg5 b5 10. Nxb5 cxb5 11. Bxb5+ Nbd7 12. O-O-O Rd8 13. Rxd7 Rxd7 14. Rd1 Qe6 15. Bxd7+ Nxd7 16. Qb8+ Nxb8 17. Rd8#
positions.note: Paris 1858. Every White move develops a piece with a threat. Step through it; after 12.O-O-O count the roads pointing at Black's king.

lessons.name: Scholar's mate
lessons.about: Make the four-move mate, then learn to stop it, then spot its shape.

moments.name: the defence
moments.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Bc4 Nc6 3. Qh5 g6

moments.name: the mate
moments.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Bc4 Nc6 3. Qh5 Nf6 4. Qxf7#

steps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Bc4 Nc6 3. Qh5
steps.say: Three moves by White. Now look what they aim at.
Open **King houses**. f7 is the weakest square in Black's house: only the king guards it.
Open **Roads**. Two roads meet on f7: the bishop's from c4 and the queen's from h5.
Open **Shapes**. Forget the pieces and keep the shape: a big block on h5 and a small one on c4, both pointing at the square next to the king.
Open **Territory**. Two attackers on f7 and only the king to guard it, but the king cannot take back while the bishop still aims there. If it were White's move: Qxf7, checkmate.
Open **Board**. No roads drawn here: answer from memory.

ask.q: Tap the square both pieces aim at.
ask.right: Yes: f7, next to the king.

steps.say: Open **Shapes**. Blocks only. Is this the attack you just saw?

ask.q: Is this the attack on f7?
ask.right: Yes: a big block on h5 and a small one on c4.

steps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Bc4 Nc6 3. Nf3
steps.say: Open **Shapes**. Another board.

ask.q: Is this the attack on f7?
ask.right: Right: the queen is still at home, only one piece aims at f7.

steps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Bc4 Nc6 3. Qh5 Nf6 4. Qxf7#
steps.say: Black played a careless move. Open **Board**, find the strike on the board or on paper, then press ▶.
Open **King houses**. Checkmate: the king has no square to run to and nobody can take the queen.

ask.right: Yes: the queen, and the bishop guards her.

steps.say: Open **Shapes**. Blocks only again.

ask.right: Yes: the big block sits on f7, next to the king.

steps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Bc4 Nc6 3. Qh5 Nf6 4. Qxf7#
steps.say: Open **Shapes**. One more board.

ask.right: Right: the queen is still on h5. This is the threat, not the mate.

steps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Bc4 Nc6 3. Qh5 g6
steps.say: Open **Territory**. Black to move. Give f7 a defender besides the king, or chase the queen away, then press ▶.
Open **Board**. g6 blocks the queen's road. Qe7, Qf6 and Nh6 also work: each one guards f7 or chases the queen.
Open **Board**. Black to move again, and Qxf7 is coming.

ask.right: Yes: g6 blocks the queen's road and attacks the queen.

steps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Bc4 Nc6 3. Qh5 g6 4. Qf3
steps.say: Open **Shapes**. Same shape, the queen only moved. Where does it point? f7 again.

steps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Bc4 Nc6 3. Qh5 g6 4. Qf3 Nf6
steps.say: Open **Board**. The king alone is not enough again: guard f7 with a piece, then press ▶. Keep watching f7 until you castle.
Open **Shapes**. Blocks only.

ask.right: Yes: a small block on g6 stands in the queen's road.

steps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Bc4 Nc6 3. Qh5 Nf6 4. Qxf7#
steps.say: Open **Shapes**. One more board.

ask.right: Right: the knight went to f6 and the road to f7 is still open.

steps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Qh5 Nc6 3. Bc4
steps.say: Open **Shapes**. Is the mate shape here? Say which square it strikes, press Reveal pieces, then Next.
Open **Territory**. Yes: the same shape by another road. f7 again.

steps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Bc5 3. Nxe5 Qh4
steps.say: Open **Shapes**. Is the mate shape here? Say which square it strikes, press Reveal pieces, then Next.
Open **Roads**. Yes, and it is coming at you: queen h4 and bishop c5 both point at f2, and Qxf2 would be checkmate. Guard f2 or chase the queen.

steps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Bc4 Nc6 3. Nf3
steps.say: Open **Shapes**. Is the mate shape here? Say which square it strikes, press Reveal pieces, then Next.
Open **Roads**. No. The queen is still at home, so only one road reaches f7. One attacker against one defender is no mate.

lessons.name: Eyes on f7
lessons.about: Ten openings: which two pieces aim at the square next to the king?

steps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Bc4 Nc6 3. Qh5
steps.say: Ten boards from the first moves. Each time ask: which blocks aim at the square next to the king, f7 or f2? Two pieces there is the danger sign.

steps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Bc4 Nc6 3. Qh5
steps.say: Open **Shapes**. Board 1 of 10. Blocks only: look at the square next to each king.
Open **Roads**. Queen h5 and bishop c4: two roads crossing on f7. Only the king guards it, so Qxf7 would be mate.

steps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Bc4 Nc6 3. Nf3
steps.say: Open **Shapes**. Board 2 of 10. Blocks only: look at the square next to each king.
Open **Territory**. Only the bishop points at f7 and the king guards it: one against one, nothing yet.

steps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Bc4 Nc6 3. Qf3
steps.say: Open **Shapes**. Board 3 of 10. Blocks only: look at the square next to each king.
Open **Roads**. Queen f3 and bishop c4. The queen's road comes from the other side, the target is the same: Qxf7 would be mate.

steps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Qh5 Nc6
steps.say: Open **Shapes**. Board 4 of 10. Blocks only: look at the square next to each king.
Open **Territory**. The queen alone looks at f7: if it takes, the king takes back. One attacker is never enough.

steps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Bc4 Nc6 3. c3 Nf6 4. Qb3
steps.say: Open **Shapes**. Board 5 of 10. Blocks only: look at the square next to each king.
Open **Roads**. Queen b3 behind bishop c4 on one road: two attackers lined up. If the bishop takes on f7, the queen follows.

steps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Bc4 Nc6 3. Qe2
steps.say: Open **Shapes**. Board 6 of 10. Blocks only: look at the square next to each king.
Open **Roads**. Two pieces out, but the queen on e2 looks along the e-file, not at f7. Only the bishop aims there: nothing yet.

steps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bc4 Nf6 4. Ng5
steps.say: Open **Shapes**. Board 7 of 10. Blocks only: look at the square next to each king.
Open **Roads**. Knight g5 and bishop c4 both reach f7. No mate here, but Nxf7 would fork the queen and the rook.

steps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Bc4 Nc6 3. Qh5 Qe7
steps.say: Open **Shapes**. Board 8 of 10. Blocks only: look at the square next to each king.
Open **Territory**. The full shape, but Qe7 guards f7: two against two. Taking on f7 now loses the queen. Count the defenders first.

steps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Bc5 3. Nxe5 Qh4
steps.say: Open **Shapes**. Board 9 of 10. Blocks only: look at the square next to each king.
Open **Roads**. Black's turn to aim: queen h4 and bishop c5 point at f2, and Qxf2 would be mate. Guard f2 or chase the queen.

steps.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Bc4 Bc5 3. Nc3 Qf6
steps.say: Open **Shapes**. Board 10 of 10. Blocks only: look at the square next to each king.
Open **Roads**. Queen f6 down the open f-file and bishop c5: both on f2, and Qxf2 would be mate. White must guard it now.
